strings.hasawi-lomi-history.title: A History of the Hasawi Lime: From Southeast Asia to the Groves of Al-Ahsa
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.description: The Hasawi lomi's journey through history, with sources: its botanical identity, its first homeland, how it reached eastern Arabia, what its name Bin Zuhairi means, and the truth behind the Al-Ahsa versus Qatif question.
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.0.q: Is the Hasawi lime a species unique to Al-Ahsa?
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.0.a: No. It is a local landrace of the acid lime known scientifically as Citrus × aurantiifolia, a natural hybrid that arose in Southeast Asia and reached Al-Ahsa through trade and seafaring. What sets Al-Ahsa apart is centuries of local selection and the customs built around the fruit, not the origin of the species.
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.1.q: When did the acid lime reach Al-Ahsa?
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.1.a: No historical document dates its arrival in Al-Ahsa specifically. The best-documented account concerns the neighbourhood: the lime has been grown in Oman for at least 4 centuries, brought by Arab sailors, according to a study published in SpringerPlus in 2016.
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.2.q: What is the difference between the Hasawi lime and the Qatifi lime?
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.2.a: They are two names for one fruit, according to official Saudi sources: the Saudi Press Agency and Saudipedia both record that the Hasawi lime is also called the Qatifi lime and Bin Zuhairi. The difference is in the name, not the plant.
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.3.q: What does the name Bin Zuhairi mean?
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.faq.3.a: The word is of Persian origin and means 'antidote', as recorded in Al-Mu'jam Al-Wasit. Its compound root is 'badzahr', the same word that entered European languages as 'bezoar'.
strings.hasawi-lomi-history.body:
When the scent of lomi drifts through the homes of Al-Ahsa in summer, it feels as if this small green fruit has grown here since the beginning of time. Its true story is longer and travels further: it begins in the forests of Southeast Asia millions of years ago, passes through trading ships and Arab sailors, and ends in the groves of the oasis, where the [Hasawi lomi](/tr/blog/hasawi-lomi-lime/) has become the second agricultural product after dates.

This article tells that journey with sources: every fact is paired with a link to its reference, and where something is unproven, we say so. The oasis needs no legend to be proud of its lime.

## What Is the Hasawi Lime, Botanically?

The Hasawi lime is not a species of its own, but a local landrace of the small acid lime known around the world by several names: Key lime, Mexican lime and West Indian lime, with the scientific name Citrus × aurantiifolia. In Oman it is the Omani lime, in Egypt the banzahir, and in eastern Arabia the lomi ([Wikipedia: Key lime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_lime) and the [NC State Extension plant guide](https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/citrus-x-aurantiifolia/)).

In official Saudi sources, the [Saudi Press Agency](https://www.spa.gov.sa/a2a7e0ca4bw) and [Saudipedia](https://saudipedia.com/article/15994/) both record that the Hasawi lime "is called the Qatifi lime and Bin Zuhairi", meaning the three names belong to a single fruit.

The most important point about its identity: this "species" is not a true wild species but a **natural hybrid** of two wild parents, Citrus micrantha of the papeda group and Citrus medica, the citron, which is why its name carries the hybrid sign (×). Genomic analysis has confirmed this hybrid origin ([Wikipedia: Key lime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_lime) and [Wu et al., Nature, 2018](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25447)).

This distinction is decisive for the history: the first hybridisation happened where both parents grew together, a tropical Asian environment, and neither parent grows wild in eastern Arabia. Every lomi tree in Al-Ahsa is therefore, by necessity, descended from a tree that arrived from outside.

## The First Homeland: Southeast Asia and the Himalayan Foothills

The landmark genomic study published in [Nature in 2018](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25447), based on 60 genomes representing the ancestral lineages of citrus, concluded that the genus diversified in the late Miocene through a rapid radiation in Southeast Asia, linked to a marked weakening of the monsoon.

A [later genomic review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12203252/) narrows the centre of origin further: the southeastern Himalayan region spanning eastern Assam in India, western Yunnan in China and Myanmar, some 7 to 8 million years ago. The acid lime in particular is native to the tropics of Southeast Asia according to the [NC State Extension guide](https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/citrus-x-aurantiifolia/).

The common phrase "it comes from India and the Malay Archipelago" is therefore imprecise: India was a corridor and a centre of dispersal, not the first homeland.

## The Journey West: 3 Waves Across a Thousand Years

Citrus did not reach the West in a single wave, but in several separated by centuries. The 2017 study [The Citrus Route Revealed](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/318556307_The_Citrus_Route_Revealed_From_Southeast_Asia_into_the_Mediterranean) traced the sequence from botanical and archaeological remains:

- **The citron** moved west first, through Persia and the Levant; its remains were found in a Persian royal garden near Jerusalem dating to the 5th and 4th centuries BCE.
- **The lemon** followed; its oldest remains were found in the Roman Forum in the late 1st century BCE.
- **The acid lime**, together with the sour orange and the pomelo, did not reach the Mediterranean basin until the 10th century CE, as part of the great agricultural diffusion of the Islamic world.

This third wave is the heart of historian [Andrew Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Murray_Watson)'s thesis in Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World (700 to 1100), which traced the spread of 17 food crops, the acid lime and the sour orange among them, through irrigation networks and agricultural knowledge in the first four centuries of Islamic rule.

## When Did It Reach Eastern Arabia?

Here begins the part where stories multiply and documents thin out, and honesty requires drawing its limits clearly.

**What is documented:** the best available account concerns the immediate neighbourhood, not Al-Ahsa itself. A [study published in SpringerPlus in 2016](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5047875/) records that the Omani lime has been cultivated in Oman for at least 4 centuries, that it was brought there by Arab sailors, and that it remained Oman's second most important fruit crop after dates until the 1970s.

**What is not documented:** no document or historical text dates the arrival of the acid lime in the Al-Ahsa or Qatif oases specifically, and no published archaeobotanical evidence (seed remains or pollen) from archaeological sites in eastern Arabia proves the presence of citrus in any particular period. The claim that citrus entered both oases at the same time is a reasonable inference from their shared environment and trade network, not an established fact.

The likeliest reading, then, is that the lomi reached the Arabian Gulf coast the same way it reached Oman: by sea, with merchants and sailors, at a date we cannot yet fix.

## Al-Ahsa or Qatif? A Question That Needs No Quarrel

It is sometimes said that the tree originated in one of the two oases and then spread to the other. That claim fails on 3 independent grounds:

1. **Botanical:** the species is a hybrid of Asian origin and neither wild parent exists in eastern Arabia, so a local origin is biologically impossible, not merely unlikely ([Wikipedia: Key lime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_lime)).
2. **Linguistic:** the two names belong to one fruit, as the [Saudi Press Agency](https://www.spa.gov.sa/a2a7e0ca4bw) and [Saudipedia](https://saudipedia.com/article/15994/) confirm; the difference is in the name, not the plant.
3. **Genetic:** the acid lime across the region is propagated from very closely related stock. An [AFLP analysis of acid lime in Oman](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29527419/) found its genetic diversity so low that this was suggested as a factor in the spread of witches' broom disease. Low diversity means, in practice, that the region's trees are near-copies of a single genetic stock, not distinct landraces that each arose in its own oasis.

So what remains for the two oases? Something worth more than a claim of origin: centuries of local agricultural selection, an irrigation system and palm shade that created a microclimate of their own, inherited know-how in pruning, sun-drying and ageing, and a complete food culture crowned by the custom of jameed. That is what distinction is built on, not the tree of origin.

As for the differences attributed to the two oases' produce in peel thickness, acidity and essential oils, they are an environmentally plausible hypothesis, but no published comparative study has measured them, so they remain a matter of likelihood.

## Where Does the Name Bin Zuhairi Come From?

The fruit's very name carries a trace of its journey. The word banzahir is of Persian origin and means **antidote**, a meaning recorded explicitly in [Al-Mu'jam Al-Wasit](https://www.almaany.com/ar/dict/ar-ar/بنزهير/). Its compound root is badzahr: bad meaning "against" and zahr meaning "poison", the same word that entered European languages as bezoar, the antidote stone ([dictionary of foreign loanwords in Arabic](https://mbtda.com/language/a3jmi/baa.php)).

The significance runs deeper than it looks: the fruit's name is Persian in freight, one more sign that it arrived through a trading and linguistic network spanning the region, rather than sprouting locally and being named locally. Lomi, meanwhile, is a general name across the Arabian Gulf region, and Hasawi and Qatifi are geographical labels for the market, not for the landrace.

## The Lomi Today: From Imported Fruit to Local Identity

The fruit that came from afar is today the emblem of the oasis summer. The Hasawi lomi is officially classed as Al-Ahsa's second agricultural product after dates ([Saudipedia](https://saudipedia.com/article/15994/)), and the [Saudi Press Agency](https://www.spa.gov.sa/a2a7e0ca4bw) records more than 100,000 bearing trees in the oasis, each yielding 25 to 30 kilograms a season. Tree counts do vary between official sources and some [press coverage](https://www.alwatan.com.sa/article/1084098); we use the official agency's figure here, as on our [Fruits of Al-Ahsa](/tr/fruits/) page.

Culturally, Hasawi families gather every summer to press and store the lime, most visibly as jameed: lomi juice sun-dried and aged in glass jars for use all year round, a custom handed down through the generations ([Akhbaar 24](https://www.akhbaar24.com/article/detail/615953)). The celebration has grown to the point that the fruit has its own annual [Hasawi Lomi Exhibition](/tr/events/hasawi-lomi-exhibition/), and picking it from the tree has become a visitor experience at the [Hasawi Lemon Farm](/tr/attractions/lemon-farm/).

## A Threat to the Heritage: Witches' Broom Disease

The lomi's story is incomplete without its greatest danger. Witches' broom disease of lime is caused by a phytoplasma known as Candidatus Phytoplasma aurantifolia, first detected in Oman in the 1970s, which then spread to the United Arab Emirates in 1989 and Iran in the 1990s, destroying more than a million lime trees ([European Food Safety Authority report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009860/)). Oman's lime production fell by more than 50% over 3 decades, chiefly because of it ([Plant Pathology, 2017](https://bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ppa.12683)).

What matters most for Al-Ahsa: a [study published in Plant Disease in 2021](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-10-20-2112-RE) showed that phytoplasma isolates taken from the Al-Ahsa region are genetically distinct from their counterparts elsewhere in the Middle East. Earlier, a Saudi study from 2009 (Alhudaib et al.) documented the phytoplasma associated with lime decline in the Kingdom and its likely vectors, as the [same European report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009860/) notes.

This explains why the lomi's agricultural heritage in Al-Ahsa is at once precious and fragile: a landrace of low genetic diversity in a region facing a disease that has destroyed a million trees next door.

## The Bottom Line

- The Hasawi lime is Citrus × aurantiifolia, a natural hybrid of Citrus micrantha and Citrus medica, neither a true species nor a variety of local origin.
- Its first homeland is Southeast Asia and the eastern Himalayan foothills, not India alone and not the Arabian Peninsula.
- It reached the Mediterranean in the 10th century CE with the agricultural diffusion of the Islamic world; its arrival in the Arabian Gulf region most likely came by sea and trade, as witnessed by at least 4 centuries of cultivation in Oman.
- Hasawi lime, Qatifi lime, Bin Zuhairi and lomi are names for one fruit, as official Saudi sources confirm.
- There is no basis for attributing the origin to either Al-Ahsa or Qatif; the two oases' real value lies in their accumulated agricultural and cultural heritage.

If you would like to meet this fruit yourself, its season is summer, as our [Fruits of Al-Ahsa](/tr/fruits/) page documents; the [Hasawi lomi article](/tr/blog/hasawi-lomi-lime/) is your guide to its qualities and annual exhibition, and [Plan Your Trip](/tr/plan-your-trip/) strings the groves and souqs into a single route.

strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.title: Tarafa ibn al-Abd and Al-Ahsa: What the Classical Arabic Sources Say About the Mu'allaqa Poet and Hajar
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.description: What links Tarafa ibn al-Abd to Hajar and Al-Ahsa? His end and his grave as told by Ibn Qutaybah and Ibn al-Anbari, what Hajar and al-Bahrayn mean in Yaqut al-Hamawi, and what a visitor finds today.
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.0.q: Was Tarafa ibn al-Abd born in Al-Ahsa?
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.0.a: The classical sources we consulted do not name the place where Tarafa ibn al-Abd was born. What they relate is that the letter of Amr ibn Hind was addressed to his governor over al-Bahrayn and Hajar, al-Bahrayn here being the ancient region between Basra and Oman with Hajar as its chief town, that Tarafa came to the governor while he was at Hajar, and that his grave is at Hajar, as in Ibn al-Anbari's commentary. The statement that he was born in Al-Ahsa Governorate, which used to be known as Hajar, is made by Saudipedia.
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.1.q: How are Hajar, al-Bahrayn and Al-Ahsa related?
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.1.a: For Yaqut al-Hamawi in Mu'jam al-Buldan, al-Bahrayn is a collective name for lands on the coast of the Sea of India between Basra and Oman, Hajar is a city that is the chief town of al-Bahrayn, and Al-Ahsa is a city in al-Bahrayn that was made the principal town of Hajar. So in the reports about Tarafa, al-Bahrayn is a wide region and Hajar is its chief town.
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.2.q: How did Tarafa ibn al-Abd die, and how old was he?
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.2.a: Ibn Qutaybah relates that Amr ibn Hind wrote Tarafa a letter to his governor over al-Bahrayn and let him believe it contained a reward; he carried it there and was killed. Al-Bahrayn here is the ancient region between Basra and Oman whose chief town is Hajar, as in Yaqut al-Hamawi. There are two reports of his age: he was killed at 20 according to Ibn Qutaybah, and at 26 according to al-Baghdadi in Khizanat al-Adab.
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.3.q: Is the grave of Tarafa ibn al-Abd known in Al-Ahsa today?
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.faq.3.a: Ibn al-Anbari relates that his grave is at Hajar, on a piece of its land belonging to Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba, but the report does not fix the spot, so we do not point visitors to a grave. Nor did we find a permanent landmark bearing his name; what is documented is the Tarafa ibn al-Abd Festival, organised by the Ministry of Culture at King Abdullah Environmental Park from 16 to 24 November 2023, which has ended.
strings.tarafa-ibn-al-abd.body:
«لِخَوْلةَ أَطلالٌ ببُرْقَةِ ثَهْمَدِ»: "Khawla has ruins of a camp at Burqat Thahmad." It is a half-line many Arabic speakers remember from their school days, along with the name of the man who composed it: Tarafa ibn al-Abd. What fewer remember is that the classical Arabic sources place the end of this poet's road at Hajar, and Hajar, for Yaqut al-Hamawi, is the chief town of the region in which Al-Ahsa lies.

This article gives three answers from those sources themselves: whether Tarafa ibn al-Abd was from Al-Ahsa, what Hajar and al-Bahrayn mean in the reports about him, and what remains for a visitor today. We pass on what these books relate in their own words, and we say where they fall silent.

*The image at the top of this article is an imagined, AI-generated depiction, not a portrait of the poet.*

## Who Was Tarafa ibn al-Abd?

Tarafa ibn al-Abd was a Jahili poet, that is, one of the poets from before Islam, of the tribe of Bakr ibn Wa'il, and his Mu'allaqa is the long ode on the strength of which the early critics ranked him. His lineage in [Ibn Sallam al-Jumahi](https://shamela.ws/book/6738/135) (d. 232 AH) runs: Tarafa ibn al-Abd ibn Sufyan ibn Sa'd ibn Malik ibn Dubay'a ibn Qays ibn Tha'laba, and [al-Baghdadi](https://shamela.ws/book/12732/887) (d. 1093 AH) carries it up to Bakr ibn Wa'il. [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/178) (d. 276 AH) notes that his name is said to have been Amr, that he was called Tarafa after a verse he composed, and that his mother was Warda.

He grew up an orphan. [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/177) says: "Tarafa's father had died while Tarafa was small, and his paternal uncles refused to divide his property." His Mu'allaqa has a verse on the injustice of kin:

> وظُلمُ ذَوِي القُرْبى أَشَدُّ مَضَاضة
> عَلَى المرءِ من وقع الحُسام المُهَنّدِ
>
> *The injustice of close kin stings a man more sharply than the stroke of a keen Indian sword.*

The attribution of this verse has long been disputed: [Ibn al-Anbari](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/207) (d. 328 AH) gives the verse in his commentary on the Mu'allaqa, then quotes Abu Ja'far as saying that the verse is not from Tarafa's ode but belongs to Adi ibn Zayd al-Ibadi.

His standing is high, though little of his poetry survived. Ibn Sallam put him in the fourth class of the master poets, four men who in his words "belong with the foremost, and were held back only by how little of their poetry is in the hands of the transmitters", and said of him: "[As for Tarafa, he is the best poet of all for a single poem](https://shamela.ws/book/6738/136)", meaning his Mu'allaqa. [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/175) said: "He is the finest of them in a long ode." And [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/179) relates from Abu Ubayda that Labid was asked who the best poet of the Arabs was; he named Imru' al-Qays, then said: "The 20-year-old", meaning Tarafa.

## Was Tarafa ibn al-Abd from Al-Ahsa? What the Classical Sources Say and Where They Are Silent

In the accounts of Tarafa ibn al-Abd given by Ibn Sallam, Ibn Qutaybah, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Baghdadi we found no text that names his birthplace. What these books relate is a different link to Hajar, one better anchored in the texts: it lies in his end, not in his birth.

Three passages carry that link:

- **Where the letter was addressed**: in [Ibn al-Anbari](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/121)'s account, Amr ibn Hind wrote for Tarafa and al-Mutalammis "to his governor over al-Bahrayn and Hajar", the governor being the man he had set over them. Al-Mutalammis was Tarafa's maternal uncle, as al-Baghdadi notes. Al-Bahrayn here is a wide ancient region whose chief town is Hajar; it is explained in the section on the old names below.
- **Where they met**: "[Then Tarafa travelled on until he came to the governor of al-Bahrayn, who was at Hajar](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/125)."
- **The grave**: "[His grave today is at Hajar, on a piece of its land belonging to Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/126)." Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba are his own people, as his lineage shows. "Today" here is the narrator's day, not ours.

[Yaqut al-Hamawi](https://shamela.ws/book/23735/342) (d. 626 AH) records that before its conquest al-Bahrayn held "a great many people of Abd al-Qays, Bakr ibn Wa'il and Tamim, living in its open country". That describes the region before its conquest; it is not a text about the poet's own time.

The explicit statement about his birth is a modern one: [Saudipedia](https://saudipedia.com/ar/مهرجان-طرفة-بن-العبد) says he was born "in Al-Ahsa Governorate, which used to be known as 'Hajar'". We report it as Saudipedia's statement, and set beside it the silence of the early sources.

## How Did Tarafa ibn al-Abd Die? The Story of the Letter of al-Mutalammis

Tarafa ibn al-Abd was killed young, by a letter he carried in his own hand from the king to the king's governor at Hajar, in a report known among the Arab chroniclers as "the letter of al-Mutalammis" (sahifat al-Mutalammis), the sahifa being the sealed letter that Tarafa and al-Mutalammis each carried.

Tarafa was a drinking companion of Amr ibn Hind, king of al-Hira, and he was, as [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/175) describes him, "bold in satirising them and in satirising others", meaning his own people. He satirised the king, and the satire reached the king.

Ibn al-Anbari then tells the story as follows. Al-Mutalammis and Tarafa came to Amr ibn Hind, who wrote for them to his governor over al-Bahrayn and Hajar and let them believe that the two letters contained rewards. On the road al-Mutalammis grew suspicious and proposed that they look into the letters, "but Tarafa refused to break the king's seal". Al-Mutalammis handed his letter to a boy from among the boys of al-Hira, who read it to him, and [al-Mutalammis threw the letter into the river of al-Hira and fled to Syria](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/122). Al-Mutalammis had warned Tarafa, and Tarafa answered that even if the king had dared to move against al-Mutalammis, [he would never dare to move against him](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/123).

Tarafa went on until he came to the governor at Hajar. In the account, the governor, who was related to Tarafa on the mother's side, said to him: "Flee this very night, for I have been ordered to kill you." He refused: "By God, I will never do that." So Tarafa was imprisoned; the governor held himself above killing him and wrote to the king that he would not kill the man. In Ibn al-Anbari's account the king sent another governor over al-Bahrayn and ordered him to kill Tarafa, and the one who killed him was a man of Abd al-Qays.

The names in the story are disputed: the governor is "Rabi'a ibn al-Harith al-Abdi" in Ibn al-Anbari and "al-Rabi' ibn Hawthara" in [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/179), and in one statement cited by [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/176) the killer was al-Mu'alla ibn Hanash al-Abdi. We do not choose between them.

That is why the story is best read as a report handed down by transmitters. The historian [Jawad Ali](https://shamela.ws/book/7299/1657) describes its ending as "embellished, polished storytelling related by the chroniclers", then [draws from it](https://shamela.ws/book/7299/1658): "that al-Bahrayn in that period was subject to the king of al-Hira, and that its ruler was a governor for Amr ibn Hind".

Tarafa died young, and there are two reports of his age. In [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/178): "He was killed at 20 years of age, and so he is called the 20-year-old." In al-Baghdadi: "He was killed at 26 years of age." It is as if he were describing himself when he said:

> أَرَى الموتَ يَعتامُ الكِرام ويَصْطَفي
> عَقِيلةَ مالِ الفاحشِ المتشَدِّدِ
>
> *I see death choosing out the generous, and picking for itself the best of the tight-fisted miser's wealth.*

The verb ya'tam, as [Ibn al-Anbari](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/198) explains it, means "chooses".

## Hajar, al-Bahrayn and Al-Ahsa: How to Read the Old Names

A visitor reads "al-Bahrayn" in the reports about Tarafa and assumes that some land other than Al-Ahsa is meant. What is meant is a wide ancient region. Yaqut al-Hamawi defines it in [Mu'jam al-Buldan](https://shamela.ws/book/23735/342) as "a collective name for lands on the coast of the Sea of India between Basra and Oman", and quotes Abu Ubayda for its places: "al-Khatt, al-Qatif, al-Ara, Hajar, Baynuna, al-Zara, Jawatha, al-Sabur, Darin and al-Ghaba", adding that "the principal town of Hajar is al-Safa and al-Mushaqar".

[Hajar](https://shamela.ws/book/23735/2426), for him, is "a city, and it is the chief town of al-Bahrayn", and he adds: "It is also said that the whole district of al-Bahrayn is Hajar, and that is the correct view."

And where does Al-Ahsa stand in this? Yaqut says in [its entry](https://shamela.ws/book/23735/107): "Al-Ahsa: a city in al-Bahrayn, well known and famous", and records that the man who built it up and fortified it made it "the qasaba of Hajar", that is, its principal town, and that in his own time it was "a famous, flourishing city". The name itself comes from water: al-Ahsa is [the plural of hisy](https://shamela.ws/book/23735/106), "which is the water that the ground soaks up from the sand", so that the Arabs dig down for it and draw it out. He also quotes al-Azhari as saying that al-Bahrayn was so named because "in the area of its villages there is a small lake at the gate of Al-Ahsa".

So when the account says Tarafa came to the governor "who was at Hajar", it is speaking of the chief town of this region. The city of Al-Ahsa by name is mentioned in Yaqut as the principal town of Hajar, not as a place in the report about the poet.

## The Mu'allaqa of Tarafa ibn al-Abd: Ships and a Sailor from Hajar

The closest the Mu'allaqa of Tarafa ibn al-Abd comes to Hajar is a seafaring image near its opening, where he likens the camel litters of the departing women to ships:

> كأَنَّ حُدُوجَ المالكيّةِ غُدْوةً
> خَلايا سَفِينٍ بالنَّواصِف من دَدِ
>
> عَدَوْلِيّةٌ أو مِنْ سَفِينِ ابنِ يامِنٍ
> يَجُورُ بها المَلاَّحُ طَوْراً ويَهْتدِي
>
> يَشُقُّ حَبَابَ الماءِ حَيزومُها بهَا
> كما قَسَمَ التُّربَ المُفايِلُ باليَدِ
>
> *As if the litters of the Malikite woman, at morning, were great ships in the broad channels of Dad,*
>
> *Adawli ships, or ships of Ibn Yamin, which the sailor now lets stray and now steers true,*
>
> *her prow cleaving the ripples of the water as a player of the game of fiyal parts the dust with his hand.*

[Ibn al-Anbari](https://shamela.ws/book/124335/135) explains "Adawli" with several views: one, that the ships are named after an island called Adawla, below Awal; another, that they are named "after a people who used to settle at Hajar". He then says: "And Ibn Yamin: a sailor from the people of Hajar as well." So the name of Hajar is present in the commentary on the Mu'allaqa, not in the wording of the verse.

The third verse, the one about the ship's prow cutting the water, is counted by [Ibn Qutaybah](https://shamela.ws/book/23785/180) among "what Tarafa was first to say and others took from him", and he notes that Labid and al-Tirimmah took it.

A poet who knows how a ship's prow parts the water: an image that suits a region where the sands meet the coast.

## Tarafa ibn al-Abd in Al-Ahsa Today: What Does a Visitor Find?

We begin with what you will not find: the reports say his grave is "at Hajar" and fix no spot, so there is no grave we can point you to. Nor did we find a street, a monument or a recurring event in Al-Ahsa that carries his name.

There is one documented trace, and it has passed: the **Tarafa ibn al-Abd Festival**. [Saudipedia](https://saudipedia.com/ar/مهرجان-طرفة-بن-العبد) records that the Ministry of Culture organised it to introduce the poet's character and his life in poetry, that it received its guests at King Abdullah Environmental Park from 16 to 24 November 2023, and that one of its aims was "to strengthen the ties between the early Arab poets and their geographical sites".

What remains for you:

- **[King Abdullah Environmental Park](/tr/attractions/king-abdullah-park/)**: the site of the festival. Details for visiting are on its page.
- **Two names from Yaqut's text** have pages on our site: [Jawatha](/tr/attractions/jawatha-mosque/) and [al-Mushaqar](/tr/attractions/mushaqar/). We link name to name, and do not claim that the poet stood at either of them.
- For the history of the oasis: [Al-Ahsa Museum](/tr/attractions/ahsa-museum/), with no claim of a link to the poet.
- For the coast that the ship verses call to mind: [Al-Uqair](/tr/attractions/al-uqair/), a link of scenery, not of record.

And if the cultural side of the oasis draws you, our article on [the living crafts of Al-Ahsa](/tr/blog/al-ahsa-traditional-crafts/) completes the picture.

## The Bottom Line

- Tarafa ibn al-Abd was of Bakr ibn Wa'il, "the best poet of all for a single poem" in Ibn Sallam, and "the finest of them in a long ode" in Ibn Qutaybah.
- The classical sources we consulted do not name his birthplace; the statement that he was born in Al-Ahsa is made by Saudipedia.
- In Ibn al-Anbari's account the king's letter was addressed to his governor over al-Bahrayn and Hajar, Tarafa came to him at Hajar, and his grave is at Hajar on land belonging to his people.
- Hajar, in Yaqut, is the chief town of al-Bahrayn, and Al-Ahsa is a city in al-Bahrayn that was made the principal town of Hajar.
- He was killed young: at 20 in one report, and at 26 in another.
- The commentary on his Mu'allaqa has a sailor from the people of Hajar, and a verse on the ship that he was first to say and later poets took.
- There is no identified grave and no permanent landmark in his name today, as far as we found; what is documented is the Ministry of Culture's festival in November 2023 at King Abdullah Environmental Park.

Read the opening of the Mu'allaqa once more while you are in the oasis. The ruins the poet wept over are not on our map, but Hajar, where the books say his road ended, is in Yaqut an old name for this very district.
